name: Constitutional delay of growth

card.summary: A normal developmental variant in which puberty and the growth spurt start later than peers, so height and features catch up in the later teens.
card.aka: CDGP, constitutional delay of growth and puberty, late bloomer
card.note: Delayed puberty has other possible causes; a clinician's assessment distinguishes them.

quick.overview:
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP) is a pattern in which a teenager starts puberty later than most peers but otherwise develops normally. Because the growth spurt, voice change and facial maturation arrive late, a late bloomer can look younger and shorter than classmates for several years.

Paediatric endocrinology reviews describe it as the most common cause of delayed puberty, especially in boys, and note that growth typically continues for longer, so many catch up. How much adult height is gained back is described as varying between studies.
quick.how: In practice, clinicians usually assess growth charts, family history of late puberty, and a bone-age X-ray, and many cases are simply monitored. For boys with marked delay or distress, specialists sometimes use a short course of low-dose testosterone to start puberty; aromatase inhibitors have been studied in trials. Online, late bloomers discuss waiting for later growth and tracking it.
quick.risks: The main reported downsides are psychosocial: higher rates of anxiety or low mood have been described in boys with delayed puberty. Treatments carry their own effects, and bone age is monitored to avoid closing the growth plates early. Other conditions, such as hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, can resemble CDGP in early adolescence and are ruled out by a clinician.

lead: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP), often called being a late bloomer, is a variation of normal development in which puberty begins later than average and the pubertal growth spurt follows later too. Reviews in paediatric endocrinology describe it as the most frequent cause of delayed puberty, particularly in boys.[2][4]

For appearance, it matters because late puberty postpones height gain, muscle development, facial bone and jaw maturation, and voice change. Teens affected often look younger than peers for a time, then continue growing after others have stopped. Reviews note that bone age is delayed in proportion, which is the basis for the expectation of later catch-up growth.[3][4]

Evaluation typically combines growth history, family pubertal timing, bone-age imaging and sometimes hormone tests. Distinguishing CDGP from congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism can be difficult in early adolescence because the two look alike.[1] Treatment ranges from monitoring to short, specialist-supervised hormone courses; trials have also studied aromatase inhibitors for adult height.[6][7]

angle.text: A late bloomer's height, jaw and body development arrive on a delayed schedule, so appearance relative to peers often improves in the later teens. Teens and families use growth charts and bone-age assessment to understand where they are on that schedule.

paras: Puberty is usually called delayed when it has not begun by an age about two standard deviations later than average. In constitutional delay, children are shorter than peers through childhood and their height is in line with a delayed bone age, indicating that skeletal growth potential remains.[3][4] Heredity is a strong factor, and a parent who was a late bloomer is a common finding.[2]

Because the pubertal growth spurt, muscle gain, voice deepening and facial maturation are driven by sex hormones, a late start means they are all pushed later. Late bloomers therefore often look younger than classmates during the mid-teens and then undergo a period of rapid change. Paediatric reviews describe the main concerns as psychosocial, including anxiety, self-image and peer comparison, rather than long-term physical illness.[2][4]

Assessment normally includes plotting growth, checking parental pubertal timing and mid-parental height, and a hand and wrist X-ray for bone age.[3][4] Hormone measurements are used to look for pituitary or gonadal causes. Reviews of congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism note that the clinical picture can mirror CDGP in early adolescence, which makes differentiation difficult.[1]

Many reviews describe reassurance and watchful monitoring as the usual approach.[2][3] When delay is pronounced or distressing, specialists may offer a short course of testosterone in boys to start puberty, with bone age monitored.[4] Aromatase inhibitors, which reduce estrogen's effect on growth-plate closure, have been tested in randomised trials in boys with delayed puberty and short stature.[6][7] Growth hormone has been studied in idiopathic short stature more broadly.[5]

The traditional view is that late bloomers catch up because they grow for longer. Some studies report final heights somewhat below genetic target, and results vary with family height and treatment, so adult outcome is described as variable in the literature.[3][4]

Randomised and controlled trials have examined aromatase inhibitor therapy in boys with delayed puberty or short stature for effects on predicted and adult height.[6][7] Another randomised trial examined hormone levels as predictors of the growth response during puberty-promoting treatment.[8] Clinical reviews summarise diagnosis and treatment of delayed puberty.[2][3][4] A growth hormone trial in idiopathic short stature measured adult height outcomes.[5]
